title: Section 104 — Punishment for murder by life-convict

content.overview: BNS s. 104 — Punishment for murder by life-convict.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Punishment for murder by life-convict. BNS restatement of IPC 303. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 303. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 104 is the rule on “Punishment for murder by life-convict”. The section provides that whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person’s natural life. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 104 exists so that “Punishment for murder by life-convict” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
104. Whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person’s natural life

Essential ingredients

learningObjectives: Understand the sentencing framework for murder committed by a person undergoing life imprisonment under BNS s. 104.
Analyze the constitutional history: how BNS s. 104 cures the unconstitutionality of old IPC s. 303 struck down in Mithu v. State of Punjab.
Recognize the dual sentencing options: death or imprisonment for life for the remainder of natural life.
Appreciate the definition of life imprisonment in this context.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 104 provides that whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life, and shall also be liable to fine.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Provides aggravated sentencing options for recidivist murderers already serving life sentences while preserving essential judicial discretion between capital punishment and imprisonment for the remainder of natural life.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 104 (replacing unconstitutional IPC s. 303).
Threshold predicate: Accused is already under a sentence of imprisonment for life.
Offence: Commits murder (as defined in s. 101).
Sentencing options: Death OR imprisonment for life meaning the remainder of natural life, and fine.
Constitutional compliance: Replaces mandatory death penalty with judicial discretion, conforming with Articles 14 and 21.
essentialIngredients: The accused was under a valid sentence of imprisonment for life at the time of the act.
The accused committed murder as defined under Section 101.
The murder was committed while the life sentence was legally subsisting (whether inside prison, on parole, or on bail).
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 104 cures one of the most famous constitutional defects in Indian penal history. Under colonial IPC Section 303, any life convict who committed murder was subjected to a mandatory death penalty with zero judicial discretion. In Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983), the Supreme Court struck down IPC 303 as unconstitutional under Articles 14 and 21 because mandatory death strips judges of sentencing discretion. BNS Section 104 addresses this defect by enacting a constitutionally valid provision: it provides two judicial options—death OR imprisonment for the remainder of the person's natural life, along with fine. This ensures judicial discretion is exercised based on mitigating and aggravating circumstances while preventing life convicts from committing murders with impunity.
examples: Teaching example (Prison murder by life convict): An inmate serving a life sentence for murder fatally stabs a prison guard during an escape attempt. Under s. 104, the court has the statutory discretion to sentence him either to death or to imprisonment for the remainder of his natural life.

Teaching example (Murder while on parole): A convict serving life imprisonment is released on temporary parole and commits a premeditated murder. Section 104 applies because the life sentence was legally subsisting.
distinctions: Section 104 vs Section 103(1): Section 103(1) applies to general offenders; Section 104 specifically applies to offenders already under sentence of life imprisonment.
Section 104 vs Old IPC 303: IPC 303 mandated death only (struck down); Section 104 provides judicial choice between death and imprisonment for the remainder of natural life.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a life convict who committed murder while on furlough can challenge the application of s. 104 on the ground that IPC 303 was unconstitutional.
Rule: BNS s. 104 cures the constitutional defect of IPC 303 by providing judicial discretion between death and natural life imprisonment.
Application: The accused was legally under sentence of life imprisonment when he committed the murder.
Conclusion: The accused is properly chargeable under BNS s. 104.
